newsitem.title: UK: U.S. ruling on Lloyd's not significant - lawyer.
newsitem.headline: U.S. ruling on Lloyd's not significant - lawyer.

text.p: A U.S. court ruling about where cases against Lloyds of London can be heard was not significant and was likely to lead to a further round of appeals, a UK lawyer said on Monday.
"This is a point of jurisdiction, which has been batting to and fro for years. This ruling is not significant in its own right," David Tiplady, insurance expert at D.J. Freeman, told Reuters.
On Thursday a federal appeals court revived a lawsuit by U.S. investors in Lloyd's of London, clearing the way for a trial against Lloyd's in a U.S. federal court.
A spokesman for the insurance market said lawyers were examining the ruling, but it was likely that Lloyd's would seek a re-hearing of the case.
"It is of concern. It goes against a run of five other cases on the same point," he added.
Friday's ruling concerns a procedural question over whether litigation against Lloyd's of London should be heard in the U.S. or England.
All Names, the traditional individual backers of Lloyd's, agree when they join the Society that any legal disputes will be heard in England.

However, in 1994, several hundred American Names sued Lloyd's in U.S. federal court for securities fraud and other claims. They alleged that Lloyd's pushed large liabilities on them without full disclosure.

In 1995, the district court hearing the case dismissed the complaint. In its decision, the district court held that the remedies available in Britain were sufficient to protect the American investors. It also ruled that there was not enough evidence to support allegations that certain Lloyd's agreements with the Names were obtained by fraud.
Last year, nearly 95 percent of Names worldwide accepted a litigation settlement offer from Lloyd's.
